newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Firm diesel widens 180/380-grade fuel oil spread.
newsitem.headline: Firm diesel widens 180/380-grade fuel oil spread.

text.p: Rising price of gas oil (diesel), which is used as feedstock for blending 380-centistoke fuel oil to the 180-grade, has made the better quality fuel oil relatively more expensive, traders said on Wednesday.

They said poor demand for 380-centistoke fuel oil, a major bunker fuel for ships, has also dampened its value and forced the price differential between the two grades to widen to around $6.25-$7.00 per tonne, up from $5.50-$6.00 two weeks ago.

The price of 180-centistoke bunker fuel is now around $103 per tonne while, the 380-grade is around $96.00. Cargo prices for the 180-grade is around $97.00 per tonne, and the 380-grade is around $91.00.

"The costs of blending have increased as prices of diesel have firmed," a bunker trader said. Diesel is used as a blending or cutter stock to reduce the viscosity or waxy texture of the 380-grade fuel oil into the 180-grade.
Traders said gas oil prices have remained strong due to sustained buying support by a group of Singapore traders who have bought nearly 14 million barrels over the past one month.
Singapore gas oil prices have risen to $27.00 per barrel this week, up from $26.65 a week ago.
"The purchases have boosted gas oil prices and have finally taken its toll on blending costs," a local trader said.
Poor bunker demand have also contributed to the differential, traders said.
"As ships normally use 380-cst supplies, poor enquiries have placed pressure on prices," another bunket trader said.
"At least two majors have been dumping a lot of 380-centistoke bunker supplies recently as demand dwindles," an independent bunker trader said.
They said the poor demand is a result of fewer ships calling at Singapore port amid high freight costs and shippers buying only smaller bunker lots.
"Shippers are not in a hurry to buy, they are buying only when necesssary," one trader said.
Another trader said most ships were also refuelling outside port limits, forcing down bunker sales in Singapore.
